journey.title: Three systems
journey.body: Built OnSight and TuneIt back to back — an examination platform and a music sequencing engine — then began Strata in August: project memory for AI-assisted coding. Each forced a different part of engineering: security, algorithmic throughput, and what an agent can be trusted to know.

projects.title: TuneIt
projects.subtitle: Algorithmic Music Flow Sequencer & Energy Optimizer
projects.summary: A sequencer that orders a playlist the way a DJ would: harmonically compatible, with a deliberate energy curve across the set.
projects.problem: Playlist ordering is usually left to shuffle or to recency. Neither respects musical key or energy, so sets lurch between incompatible tracks and flatten out emotionally.
projects.objective: Order an arbitrary playlist so consecutive tracks are harmonically compatible and the overall energy follows an intentional trajectory — at a throughput that makes it interactive rather than a batch job.
projects.architecture: A TypeScript/Express REST API fronts four independent sequencing engines. Track metadata is fetched from the YouTube Data API in batches of 12, rate-limited through Bottleneck, enriched by Google Gemini, and cached in PostgreSQL via Prisma so repeat analyses cost nothing. A Next.js 16 client renders the resulting energy trajectory and previews audio in-browser.
implementation: Four algorithmic sequencing engines built on Camelot wheel harmonic matching plus regression-based energy optimisation.

Engine behaviour checked against arousal- and valence-annotated fixtures held in the repository, in the shape of the MusAV and MTG-Jamendo annotation formats. The runs against the published datasets themselves were not recorded, so the fixtures are what the numbers below come from.
Express.js/TypeScript REST API with 12-track batching and Bottleneck rate limiting across the YouTube Data and Gemini APIs.
PostgreSQL + Prisma caching layer for track analysis results.
Next.js 16 frontend with interactive energy-trajectory visualisation and in-browser audio preview.
Google OAuth 2.0 for playlist synchronisation.

metrics.label: Frame, Drift and Rise at N=500

challenges.challenge: Third-party API quotas made per-track analysis untenable at playlist scale.
challenges.resolution: Batched requests 12 at a time behind a Bottleneck limiter and cached every analysed track in PostgreSQL, so the quota cost of a playlist falls to near zero on re-analysis.

challenges.challenge: Harmonic compatibility and energy shape pull against each other — the most compatible next track is often the wrong energy.
challenges.resolution: Separated the two concerns into distinct engines and scored candidates on a weighted objective, which let the trade-off be tuned rather than hard-coded.

projects.lessons: Caching is an architecture decision, not an optimisation. Deciding where the cache lived — at the analysed-track boundary rather than the request boundary — is what makes a second look at the same playlist cost nothing instead of a full quota of third-party calls.
projects.metricsCaption: Medians of five runs of the repository's own scale benchmark at N=500. The pool is built by duplicating 50 base tracks with jitter, so the absolute smoothness figures are optimistic — the comparison between engines is the result, not any single number. Throughput is deliberately not quoted: across the same five runs one engine measured between 82,000 and 172,000 tracks a second, which is warm-up and garbage collection rather than algorithm.

evidence.caption: Four engines, one pool, N=500
evidence.note: Unhinged's 56 broken transitions are the engine working rather than failing — it is the one allowed to break continuity. Rise keeps every track and scores highest, which is the honest caveat on the whole table: on a pool this uniform, the engine that reorders least wins.

projects.title: OnSight
projects.subtitle: Automated Examination & Assessment Platform
projects.summary: Turns a PDF question paper into a running, graded, audited online examination.
projects.problem: Setting up an online exam usually means re-typing an existing paper into a form builder, then trusting an ad-hoc grading script and a permissions model that was never really designed.
projects.objective: Ingest an existing PDF paper directly into a structured exam, grade submissions reliably inside enforced time windows, and make every access attempt auditable.
projects.architecture: A Node.js/Express service over MongoDB with Mongoose. Gemini's multimodal API handles PDF-to-MCQ extraction behind a JSON schema validator; a separate grading engine owns evaluation, timing enforcement and analytics; a hierarchical RBAC layer with JWT and refresh-token rotation guards every endpoint.
implementation: PDF-to-MCQ ingestion pipeline on Gemini multimodal APIs, with JSON schema validation, input sanitisation, and fallback handling for transient extraction failures.
Grading engine that evaluates submissions, enforces exam time windows, and computes question-level performance analytics.
Post-exam grace-mark recalculation across an already-graded cohort.
Hierarchical RBAC with JWT authentication and refresh-token rotation.
Endpoint rate limiting and persistent audit logging of unauthorised access attempts.

challenges.challenge: Multimodal extraction fails non-deterministically — a paper that parses cleanly once may not the next time.
challenges.resolution: Validated every extraction against a JSON schema and wrapped the call in explicit fallback handling, so a transient failure degrades to a retry path instead of a corrupt exam.

challenges.challenge: Grades sometimes have to change after the fact, without losing the original submission record.
challenges.resolution: Made grace-mark handling a recalculation pass over stored submissions rather than a mutation of stored grades, keeping the original record intact and auditable.

projects.lessons: Anything an LLM produces has to be treated as untrusted input. The schema validator and the fallback path are not defensive extras here — they are the feature that makes the pipeline usable.
projects.metricsCaption: These describe capabilities that exist in the implementation, not measurements. Nothing here has been benchmarked, and the record says so rather than dressing a feature list as a result.

projects.title: BobAI
projects.subtitle: Natural-Language Full-Stack Application Generator
projects.summary: Describe an application in plain English; get a provisioned repository with a working multi-tier app in it.
projects.problem: Code generators tend to stop at a snippet. The gap between a generated file and a repository you can actually run is where the time goes.
projects.objective: Take a natural-language specification all the way to a provisioned GitHub repository containing a coherent multi-tier application with a matching SQL schema.
projects.architecture: A Flask REST API drives a modular scaffolding engine that targets vanilla JS, React, and Node/Express tiers. Gemini generates source, which a multi-file extraction pipeline splits with regex fallbacks; Pexels supplies contextual assets and design tokens; PyGithub provisions and pushes the repository; subprocess-driven integration tests verify the result.
implementation: Flask REST API and modular scaffolding engine producing multi-tier applications across vanilla JS, React, and Node/Express, with generated SQL schemas.
Multi-file code extraction pipeline over Gemini output, with regex fallbacks for malformed responses.
Pexels API integration injecting contextual assets and design tokens into generated source.
Repository provisioning and GitHub deployment automated with PyGithub.
Subprocess-based integration tests validating API contracts, generated-file integrity, and deployment failure handling.

challenges.challenge: Model output does not reliably respect file boundaries, so a single malformed response can corrupt a whole generated project.
challenges.resolution: Built extraction as a pipeline with regex fallbacks at each stage, so degraded output still yields separable files rather than one unusable blob.

challenges.challenge: A generated repository that does not run is worse than no repository.
challenges.resolution: Added subprocess integration tests that exercise the API contracts and file integrity of the generated project — and the deployment failure path specifically.

projects.lessons: Testing the failure path mattered more than testing the happy path. Most of what made this reliable was deciding what should happen when generation goes wrong.
projects.metricsCaption: These describe capabilities that exist in the implementation, not measurements. The integration tests assert that generation and deployment behave; they do not produce a number, and none is claimed.

ongoing.title: Strata
ongoing.idea: A repository-local provenance framework: keep the reasoning, the dead ends and the constraints that normally evaporate once code is written, and hand an agent the minimum sufficient context instead of the whole history.
ongoing.label: Ongoing

caseFile.subtitle: Project Memory for AI-Assisted Coding
caseFile.summary: Remembers why code is the way it is: what changed, what was tried and failed, what rules a change must respect. It hands that to an AI coding agent before it starts work, with every statement labelled by how far it can be trusted.
caseFile.problem: When software is built with an AI agent, the code survives but the reasoning disappears: why one approach was chosen, which approaches failed and why, which constraints a change must keep. The next session, or the next model, starts from zero. It searches the code again, re-reads git history, and sometimes repeats a mistake that was already made and fixed.
caseFile.objective: Build a small memory that lives inside the repository, from git history, a code index and short records of intent, failed attempts and constraints, and turn it into a context pack for the task at hand: the target's current code, the commits that shaped it, whether each past decision still holds, and the relevant records. Delivered before the agent reads anything, and labelled so the agent can tell a checked fact from a claim.
caseFile.architecture: A TypeScript command-line tool on Node.js. Everything lives in .strata/ inside the repository, with no server and no cloud: records are one Markdown file per decision, and a SQLite database (Node's built-in SQLite) is a local cache that can be rebuilt. Git history, the code index and the records feed a context pack sized to a budget, 3,200 tokens by default and about 2,400 through the Claude Code hook, and the same store generates docs/strata/DECISIONS.md and FLOW.md for any agent or person. It reaches agents through a Claude Code prompt hook, an Antigravity always-on rule, and an MCP server.
implementation: A context engine that resolves a request to its target and builds the pack: current behaviour quoted from the working tree, historical decisions with what each commit replaced, constraints and previous attempts. Each pack opens with an APPLICABILITY line (SUPPORTED, PARTIAL, LOW VALUE, NOT APPLICABLE) saying how far it can answer.

Trust labels on every statement: VERIFIED (read from git or the files on disk), DECLARED (a claim someone wrote down), INFERRED (Strata's own reading) and UNKNOWN. Records are checked against git: a wrong "commit X changed file Y" is marked CONTRADICTED by git, and a record written before later changes to its files is flagged as out of date.

A code index for TypeScript and JavaScript ES modules: functions, exports, imports and call sites. JSON, Prisma, SQL, YAML and similar files are known by path and history, and the packages a package.json declares are indexed.

Records as one Markdown file per decision in .strata/records/, to be read, reviewed and committed like any document. A file that breaks the format is reported with its line number and never skipped silently, and a VERIFIED label typed by hand is read as DECLARED.

strata derive turns a Claude Code or Antigravity session transcript into a record from what the session shows (the files changed, the checks run and how they ended, what was refused) rather than by asking the agent.

One-step strata setup: initialise, index, write the docs, add the cache to .gitignore, install a post-commit hook that never fails a commit, and wire each named editor. It merges existing settings, never overwrites what it did not write, and running it again changes nothing.
An MCP server (strata mcp) exposing tools such as strata_context, strata_explain and strata_record_change, for any agent that supports MCP.
More than 770 tests, many of them building real git repositories. The known limits are kept as tests marked as expected to fail, which start failing on the day a change removes the limit.

metrics.label: History and "why" questions, Claude Code with Claude Opus
The same questions, the same agent

caseFile.metricsCaption: Measured by running the same questions with and without Strata. It cuts how much an agent searches before it answers, most on history and "why" questions; it has not been shown to make answers more correct, since without it the agent reached the same answers by reading git and the code. Simple questions cost slightly more: the pack adds about 2,400 tokens. Records are not yet measured on their own.

evidence.caption: The same questions, with and without Strata
rows: History questions on large public repositories
Questions about a project's own history
History questions on large public repositories
Fixing bugs from real bug reports
evidence.note: Results vary by task: some history questions showed no saving, and stronger models made more of the pack than cheaper ones. Early-stage software (v0.1.0), tested with Claude Code and Antigravity on Windows.

challenges.challenge: A record is someone's claim, and an agent cannot tell a checked fact from an assertion.
challenges.resolution: Every statement carries a trust label, and the one kind of claim git can settle, "commit X changed file Y", is checked: a wrong one is marked CONTRADICTED by git rather than presented as fact. What cannot be checked stays DECLARED.

challenges.challenge: Requests in plain words rarely name a file, so the target of a task is often a guess.
challenges.resolution: Requests are matched by paths, symbol names and words, and each pack opens by saying how well it matched: a vague request is labelled LOW VALUE or PARTIAL, and when nothing relevant is found Strata does not invent a target.

challenges.challenge: Context on every prompt costs tokens, even when the question is trivial.
challenges.resolution: Packs are sized to a budget, and the hook skips prompts that are only conversation and stays silent when it has nothing useful. The remaining cost, about 2,400 tokens a prompt, is listed among the known limitations rather than hidden.
